# Computer Ethics and Society

## Core ideas and reasoning

Computer ethics concerns responsible choices when using information systems. Respect privacy by collecting only necessary personal information, protecting it and using it for an agreed purpose. Copyright protects creative works; obtaining a file does not automatically grant permission to redistribute it. Follow software licence terms and attribute sources to avoid plagiarism. Accessibility means considering people with differing abilities, such as providing keyboard controls and text alternatives. Automated decisions can reproduce biases in data, so examine evidence and permit review where decisions affect people. ICT can improve communication and access to services while creating risks such as exclusion, surveillance, job displacement and electronic waste. Discuss benefits and costs with a concrete example and affected group. Ergonomics addresses healthy work practices, including screen position, suitable seating, breaks and lighting. Dispose of electronics through suitable recovery channels rather than ordinary dumping. Accessing systems without permission is not justified merely by curiosity; security testing needs explicit authorisation and a defined scope.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Explain why copying an online paragraph into an assignment without acknowledgement is problematic.

It presents another author’s work as one’s own, which is plagiarism. Attribution is required, and copyright permission or an applicable exception may also be needed.

### Example 2

State two ways to protect student privacy in a school system.

Restrict access to authorised staff according to role, and collect and retain only data needed for stated school purposes. Secure storage and transmission provide additional protection.

### Example 3

Give one positive and one negative social effect of ICT with examples.

Remote lessons can widen access for students far from school. Students without connectivity or suitable devices may be excluded, increasing inequality.
